title: C Syntax Repetition
description: Direct multiple-choice practice for C syntax and standard-library calling forms covered by the 2122 foundations, recall and midterm material.
assumptions: C17. Any standard headers needed by a snippet are included unless the question asks for the header.

Local variables have automatic storage duration unless stated otherwise. Names refer to declared objects of the stated types. Pointers, array indices and arithmetic are valid for their described use unless a question explicitly tests an error.
Bit-mask questions use 8-bit bytes and 32-bit int/unsigned int when a width is needed. Other type sizes are not assumed.

topics.title: 01 · Declarations and initialization
topics.reference: C17 declarations: type, declarator, optional initializer, semicolon.

topics.title: 02 · Literals, escapes and comments
topics.reference: Distinguish integer, character and string literals; remember C escape sequences.

topics.title: 03 · Assignment and arithmetic
topics.reference: = stores a value; arithmetic operators and compound assignments act on operands.

topics.title: 04 · Comparisons and logical operators
topics.reference: Comparisons produce int 0 or 1; && and || short-circuit.

topics.title: 05 · Grouping and precedence
topics.reference: Parentheses specify grouping; postfix operations bind before unary dereference.

topics.title: 06 · if, else and switch
topics.reference: Conditions use parentheses; braces group statements; case labels use constant expressions.

topics.title: 07 · for, while and do/while
topics.reference: Recall loop punctuation, initialization, conditions and updates.

topics.title: 08 · Functions, prototypes and calls
topics.reference: A prototype describes parameter and return types; a call supplies argument values.

topics.title: 09 · Addresses and dereferencing
topics.reference: & obtains an address; * follows a pointer; pointer objects and pointed-to objects differ.

topics.title: 10 · Pointer movement and updates
topics.reference: Pointer arithmetic advances in elements; distinguish the pointer from its target.

topics.title: 11 · Pointer layers and output arguments
topics.reference: Pass an object’s address when a function needs to modify that object, including a pointer object.

topics.title: 12 · const and pointer declarations
topics.reference: Read const relative to the pointed-to type and the pointer declarator.

topics.title: 13 · Arrays and indexing
topics.reference: Arrays contain contiguous elements. Their names usually convert to pointers in expressions.

topics.title: 14 · sizeof, counts and parameters
topics.reference: sizeof reports bytes as size_t; arrays and pointers have different size behavior.

topics.title: 15 · Characters and C strings
topics.reference: C strings end at the first null character. Capacity includes room for that terminator.

topics.title: 16 · printf conversions and arguments
topics.reference: Match the conversion to the argument after default promotions; printf receives values.

topics.title: 17 · scanf conversions and destinations
topics.reference: scanf needs correctly typed destination pointers and a conversion-result check.

topics.title: 18 · Input buffers, EOF and streams
topics.reference: Know the direct calling forms for bounded line input and standard streams.

topics.title: 19 · malloc, calloc, realloc and free
topics.reference: Allocation arguments are byte counts or count × size; check success and manage ownership.

topics.title: 20 · Byte-memory library syntax
topics.reference: memset writes bytes; memcpy requires non-overlap; memmove supports overlap.

topics.title: 21 · String-library calls
topics.reference: String calls use null-terminated character sequences; match their argument order and result contracts.

topics.title: 22 · Structures and member access
topics.reference: Use . for an object and -> for a pointer; a struct definition ends with a semicolon.

topics.title: 23 · typedef and enum
topics.reference: typedef creates an alias; enum defines named integer constants.

topics.title: 24 · Linked-node syntax
topics.reference: Self-referential structs contain pointers to their own type, and traversal updates that pointer.

topics.title: 25 · Bitwise operators and shifts
topics.reference: Use integer bitwise operators, unsigned operands, and valid shift counts.

topics.title: 26 · Set, clear, toggle and test bits
topics.reference: Bit 0 is the least significant bit. Use unsigned int x and 0 <= k < 32.

topics.title: 27 · Fields and byte indexing
topics.reference: The question supplies bit order; choose the expression that performs the one requested step.

topics.title: 28 · Casts and integer-type syntax
topics.reference: Cast before the operation when the operation’s type matters. Promotions happen before arithmetic.

topics.title: 29 · Headers, macros and guards
topics.reference: Preprocessing directives begin with #; header guards pair conditionals with an ending #endif.

topics.title: 30 · Storage, declarations and build commands
topics.reference: Distinguish declarations from definitions and compiling from linking. GCC commands here are shell commands.

questions.prompt: Declare an int named count and initialize it to zero.
questions.explanation: A declaration places the type before the name. = introduces its initializer.

questions.prompt: Declare an unsigned int named flags.
questions.explanation: unsigned modifies the integer type; it comes in the declaration specifiers.

questions.prompt: Declare two int variables, x and y, in one declaration.
questions.explanation: A comma separates declarators sharing the int type.

questions.prompt: Initialize both int variables x and y to zero.
options: int x = y = 0; /* y not previously declared */
questions.explanation: Each declarator needs its own initializer. int x, y = 0 initializes only y.

questions.prompt: Declare p as a pointer to int.
questions.explanation: The * belongs to the declarator and makes p a pointer.

questions.prompt: Declare both p and q as pointers to int.
questions.explanation: Repeat * for each pointer declarator.

questions.prompt: Which declaration makes p a pointer to int and value an ordinary int?
questions.explanation: In a comma-separated declaration, the star does not automatically apply to later names.

questions.prompt: Declare a double named average initialized to 0.0.
questions.explanation: A scalar initializer uses = after the declarator.

questions.prompt: Which spelling is a valid C identifier?
questions.explanation: An identifier may contain underscores and digits but cannot begin with a digit or be a keyword.

questions.prompt: Which punctuation ends an ordinary variable declaration?
questions.explanation: An ordinary declaration ends with a semicolon.

questions.prompt: Which is a hexadecimal integer literal?
questions.explanation: A hexadecimal integer literal begins with 0x or 0X.

questions.prompt: Which literal uses an unsigned integer suffix?
questions.explanation: u or U is an unsigned suffix; its exact resulting type also depends on the value and other suffixes.

questions.prompt: Which suffix explicitly requests long long for the integer literal 1?
questions.explanation: LL or ll requests long long; 1LL is representable in that type.

questions.prompt: Which is a character constant for the letter A?
questions.explanation: Single quotes form a character constant; double quotes form a string literal.

questions.prompt: Which is a string literal containing one visible letter?
questions.explanation: A string literal uses double quotes and includes a terminating null character.

questions.prompt: Which character constant denotes the null character?
questions.explanation: Backslash-zero denotes character value zero. The digit character is different.

questions.prompt: Which escape represents a newline inside a string?
questions.explanation: The newline escape is backslash followed by lowercase n.

questions.prompt: Which string literal contains a single backslash?
questions.explanation: A backslash in a string is escaped by another backslash.

questions.prompt: Which starts a comment that lasts to the end of the source line?
questions.explanation: C17 supports // line comments.

questions.prompt: Which writes a C block comment?
questions.explanation: A block comment starts with /* and ends with */; block comments do not nest.

questions.prompt: Assign 7 to an already declared int x.
questions.explanation: = is assignment. == compares values.

questions.prompt: Increase int x by 3 using a compound assignment.
questions.explanation: x += 3 adds three to the old value. x =+ 3 assigns positive three.

questions.prompt: Decrease int x by 2 using a compound assignment.
questions.explanation: -= subtracts and stores; =- assigns a negative value.

questions.prompt: Multiply int x by 4 and store the result in x.
questions.explanation: *= multiplies and assigns. C has no ** exponentiation operator.

questions.prompt: Divide int x by 2 and store the quotient.
questions.explanation: /= performs division and assignment. The operands here use integer division.

questions.prompt: Select the operator that gives an integer remainder.
questions.explanation: % is remainder for integer operands; the divisor must be nonzero.

questions.prompt: Increment int count by one as a complete statement.
questions.explanation: ++count changes count. count + 1 only computes an expression value.

questions.prompt: Which expression uses the old value of i, then increments i?
questions.explanation: Postfix ++ yields the old value; prefix ++ yields the incremented value.

questions.prompt: Which expression increments i and yields the new value?
questions.explanation: Prefix ++ changes the object and yields its new value.

questions.prompt: Which expression computes the negative of x without assigning to x?
questions.explanation: Unary minus computes negation. -- changes its operand.

questions.prompt: Test whether int x equals int y.
questions.explanation: == compares equality; = is assignment.

questions.prompt: Test whether int x differs from int y.
questions.explanation: != is the C inequality operator.

questions.prompt: Test whether x is at least limit.
questions.explanation: >= includes equality.

questions.prompt: Require both conditions ready and valid to hold, using a short-circuit logical operator.
questions.explanation: && treats operands as truth values and skips its right operand when the left is false.

questions.prompt: Require at least one of conditions ready and valid to hold, using a short-circuit logical operator.
questions.explanation: || is logical OR and short-circuits when the left operand is true.

questions.prompt: Negate the truth value of ready.
questions.explanation: ! is logical NOT. ~ complements individual integer bits.

questions.prompt: Which condition correctly tests that int x is strictly between 0 and 10?
questions.explanation: C does not use mathematical chained comparisons; write the two comparisons with &&.

questions.prompt: Which safely tests *p == 7 when p may be NULL or point to a valid int?
questions.explanation: && skips dereferencing p when p is NULL.

questions.prompt: Which safely tests whether int a is divisible by int b, where a >= 0 and b >= 0?
questions.explanation: The nonzero-divisor check must occur before the remainder operation.

questions.prompt: Select the conditional expression that chooses x when flag is true, otherwise y.
questions.explanation: The conditional operator is condition ? true_expression : false_expression.

questions.prompt: Group addition before multiplication.
questions.explanation: Parentheses force a + b to be evaluated as the operand of *.

questions.prompt: Test whether any bit in unsigned mask m is set in unsigned x.
questions.explanation: Equality operators bind more tightly than bitwise AND; parentheses make the mask test explicit.

questions.prompt: Which expression means dereference p, then increment that int object?
questions.explanation: Parentheses make the dereferenced object the operand of postfix ++.

questions.prompt: Which grouping describes *p++?
questions.explanation: Postfix ++ binds more tightly than unary *.

questions.prompt: Which expression means increment pointer p first, then dereference it?
questions.explanation: Prefix ++ applies to p before its result is dereferenced. The advanced pointer must be dereferenceable.

questions.prompt: Group a bitwise OR result before applying bitwise AND.
questions.explanation: Bitwise & binds more tightly than | unless parentheses override that grouping.

questions.prompt: Choose the safe grouping for a function-like macro that adds one to its argument.
questions.explanation: Parenthesize the argument and entire replacement expression; do not append a statement semicolon.

questions.prompt: Which expression takes the size of the pointed-to type rather than the pointer object?
questions.explanation: Dereference binds within sizeof here. For an ordinary non-VLA pointed-to type, no runtime dereference occurs.

questions.prompt: Execute work() only when ready is true.
questions.explanation: The condition goes in parentheses. A semicolon immediately after if creates an empty controlled statement.

questions.prompt: Choose the complete if/else syntax.
questions.explanation: else follows the controlled statement without a stray separating semicolon.

questions.prompt: Add a second condition only when the first one failed.
questions.explanation: C spells the chain as else followed by another if statement.

questions.prompt: Which symbols group several statements into one block?
questions.explanation: Braces form a compound statement.

questions.prompt: Select the switch statement header for int choice.
questions.explanation: switch takes an integer controlling expression in parentheses.

questions.prompt: Write a case label for the constant 2.
questions.explanation: A case label ends with a colon.

questions.prompt: Write the label for switch cases that did not match.
questions.explanation: default is the optional fallback label within switch.

questions.prompt: Leave the nearest enclosing switch after a case has run.
questions.explanation: break leaves the nearest switch or loop.

questions.prompt: Inside a function returning int, leave the whole function with result 0.
questions.explanation: return exits the current function and supplies its result.

questions.prompt: Which condition checks whether pointer p is null?
questions.explanation: Compare the pointer value itself with NULL; assignment changes it.

questions.prompt: Visit array indices 0 through n-1 using size_t i.
questions.explanation: The for header has three clauses separated by semicolons; i < n excludes index n.

questions.prompt: Repeat work() while ready is true, checking before each iteration.
questions.explanation: while tests before entering its body, including before the first iteration.

questions.prompt: Run work() at least once, then repeat while ready is true.
questions.explanation: The do/while form tests after the body and needs its final semicolon.

questions.prompt: Skip the rest of the current loop iteration.
questions.explanation: continue moves to the next iteration step; in for it evaluates the update clause next.

questions.prompt: Leave the nearest loop immediately.
questions.explanation: break exits the nearest enclosing loop or switch.

questions.prompt: Write a for loop with no initialization, condition or update clauses.
questions.explanation: All three clauses may be empty; their two separating semicolons remain.

questions.prompt: Traverse a valid string s from index 0, stopping at its first null character.
questions.explanation: Test the current character against the null character, then advance the index.

questions.prompt: Which loop visits an int array backward without unsigned underflow in its condition?
questions.explanation: Begin one past the last index and use i - 1 only while i is positive; this also handles n == 0.

questions.prompt: Where does the update expression ++i belong in a for header?
questions.explanation: The clauses are initialization; condition; update.

questions.prompt: Which condition keeps reading until getchar reports EOF?
questions.explanation: Parenthesize the assignment so ch receives the character or EOF, then compare. Declare ch as int.

questions.prompt: Declare a function add taking two int parameters and returning int.
questions.explanation: The prototype contains a return type, name, parenthesized parameter list, and semicolon.

questions.prompt: Define an int function twice that returns two times its int argument.
questions.explanation: A definition supplies a body directly after the declarator and returns the result.

questions.prompt: Explicitly declare that reset takes no parameters and returns no value in C17.
questions.explanation: In C17, (void) specifies no parameters; empty () in a declaration leaves parameter information unspecified.

questions.prompt: Call reset, which takes no arguments.
questions.explanation: Parentheses perform the call. void reset(); is a declaration rather than a call.

questions.prompt: Store the return value of add(x, y) in an already declared int result.
questions.explanation: A call supplies expressions, not parameter declarations.

questions.prompt: Return immediately from a function whose return type is void.
questions.explanation: A void-returning function may use return without an expression.

questions.prompt: Declare a function that takes a pointer to int and returns int.
questions.explanation: A star in the parameter declarator describes the parameter, not the return type.

questions.prompt: Declare a function that returns a pointer to int and takes no parameters.
questions.explanation: The star before the function name makes its result a pointer. (*find) would declare a function pointer object.

questions.prompt: Define the hosted-program main form with no parameters.
questions.explanation: The standard hosted form returns int; reaching its final brace also returns zero.

questions.prompt: Which parameter declaration lets a function modify a caller’s int using *out?
questions.explanation: C passes the address value as an int pointer, through which the function can change the caller’s object.

questions.prompt: Initialize int pointer p with the address of existing int x.
questions.explanation: &x produces the address of x with type int *.

questions.prompt: Read the int pointed to by valid int *p.
questions.explanation: Unary * dereferences one pointer level.

questions.prompt: Store 7 in the int pointed to by valid int *p.
questions.explanation: Assign through *p to modify the pointed-to int.

questions.prompt: Redirect int *p to the address of another int y.
questions.explanation: Assign an address to p itself to change where it points.

questions.prompt: Copy the pointer value in int *q into int *p.
questions.explanation: p = q copies an address. *p = *q copies an int between pointed-to objects.

questions.prompt: Copy the int at *q into the int at *p, leaving both pointers unchanged.
questions.explanation: Dereference on both sides copies the pointed-to value.

questions.prompt: Given int *p, what is the type of &p?
questions.explanation: Taking the address of a pointer adds a pointer layer.

questions.prompt: Given int *p, what is the type of *p?
questions.explanation: Dereferencing removes one pointer layer from the expression’s type.

questions.prompt: Which tests whether p and q point to the same address?
questions.explanation: Compare pointer values for address equality; dereferenced equality compares stored values.

questions.prompt: Given a null int pointer, which operation obtains that pointer object’s own address?
questions.explanation: The pointer object exists even when its stored value is null; taking &p does not dereference it.

questions.prompt: Advance int *p to the next array element.
questions.explanation: Incrementing a pointer moves one element, automatically accounting for the pointed-to type size.

questions.prompt: Increase the pointed-to int by one without moving p.
questions.explanation: ++*p groups as ++(*p), modifying the int.

questions.prompt: Read the current pointed-to value, then advance p by one element.
questions.explanation: Postfix ++ operates on p; dereferencing its old value reads the current element.

questions.prompt: Access the third int after the one p points to, within a valid array.
questions.explanation: p[3] is *(p + 3); indexing counts elements.

questions.prompt: Get the address of the third int after *p.
questions.explanation: Pointer addition yields an address. Dereference would yield an int object.

questions.prompt: For pointers p and q into the same int array, which expression counts the element displacement from p to q?
questions.explanation: Subtracting same-array pointers already counts elements; the result type is ptrdiff_t.

questions.prompt: If a has n elements, which expression forms its one-past pointer?
questions.explanation: One-past pointers may be formed and compared appropriately, but must not be dereferenced.

questions.prompt: Which expression dereferences the previous element, assuming it exists?
questions.explanation: Subtract from the pointer before dereferencing it.

questions.prompt: Declare pp as a pointer to a pointer to int.
questions.explanation: Two stars describe two pointer layers.

questions.prompt: Initialize int **pp to point to existing int *p.
questions.explanation: &p is the address of the pointer object and has type int **.

questions.prompt: Given valid int **pp, access the final int object.
questions.explanation: Dereference once to reach the int pointer, then again to reach the int.

questions.prompt: Change the caller’s int pointer through valid int **pp so it points to int x.
questions.explanation: *pp names the caller’s pointer object; assign the address there.

questions.prompt: Store 9 in the final int object reached through valid int **pp.
questions.explanation: Two dereferences reach the int to be changed.

questions.prompt: Call advance so it may update caller variable p.
questions.code:
void advance(int **pp);
int *p = data; /* data is a valid int array */
questions.explanation: The function needs the address of p, not p’s stored target address.

questions.prompt: Advance the caller’s pointer by one element through int **pp.
questions.explanation: *pp is the caller’s pointer. Increment that object, with a valid next array position.

questions.prompt: Which signature accepts an output parameter for a size_t count?
questions.explanation: One pointer layer suffices to write a size_t result through *out.

questions.prompt: Declare p as a pointer through which int values cannot be modified.
questions.explanation: const int * qualifies the pointed-to int. The pointer may still be reassigned.

questions.prompt: Declare a pointer p that must keep pointing to existing int x.
questions.explanation: const after * qualifies the pointer object itself.

questions.prompt: Make both p and the int accessed through p read-only via this declaration.
questions.explanation: There is a const qualifier for the pointed-to int and another for the pointer.

questions.prompt: Which statement is allowed through const int *p when y is a valid int?
questions.explanation: A pointer to const can be redirected; it cannot be used to write its target.

questions.prompt: Which statement is allowed with int *const p = &x?
questions.explanation: The pointer is fixed but its non-const target can be modified.

questions.prompt: Use a string literal through a pointer that prevents writes through that pointer.
questions.explanation: const char * communicates read-only character access; modifying a string literal is undefined regardless of pointer type.

questions.prompt: Declare a function parameter for reading a byte buffer without modifying its bytes through that parameter.
questions.explanation: Const belongs on the byte type to prevent writes through the parameter.

questions.prompt: Which pointer parameter still lets a function modify the caller’s int, while preventing reassignment of its local parameter?
questions.explanation: int *const fixes the local pointer parameter but leaves its target writable.

questions.prompt: Declare an array of five int elements.
questions.explanation: Brackets following the name give the array length.

questions.prompt: Declare an int array initialized with 2, 4 and 6, letting C infer its length.
questions.explanation: Braced elements initialize the array; omitted length is inferred here.

questions.prompt: Initialize all five int elements to zero.
questions.explanation: The first element gets zero explicitly; remaining elements are zero-initialized.

questions.prompt: Read the first element of array a.
questions.explanation: Array indexing starts at zero.

questions.prompt: Assign 7 to the third element of int array a.
questions.explanation: The third element has index 2, and = stores a value.

questions.prompt: Initialize int *p to the first element of existing int array a.
questions.explanation: In this initializer, a converts to a pointer to its first element; &a points to the whole array.

questions.prompt: Which assigns a pointer to b without trying to assign an entire array?
questions.explanation: Array objects are not assignable; pointer objects are.

questions.prompt: Declare a two-row, three-column int array.
questions.explanation: Each bracket pair supplies one array dimension.

questions.prompt: Access row 1, column 2 of int grid[2][3].
questions.explanation: Use a separate subscript for each dimension, counting each from zero.

questions.prompt: Declare p as a pointer to an entire array of three ints.
questions.explanation: Parentheses group *p so p is a pointer to an array.

questions.prompt: Declare a as an array of three pointers to int.
questions.explanation: The array declarator binds before *, making each array element a pointer.

questions.prompt: Which parameter form receives rows of three ints?
questions.explanation: The first dimension adjusts to a pointer; the column count supplies the row type.

questions.prompt: Obtain the byte size of the type int.
questions.explanation: A type name in sizeof requires parentheses.

questions.prompt: Obtain the byte size of a declared ordinary int x.
questions.explanation: sizeof may take an expression without parentheses.

questions.prompt: Count the elements of a real int array a in its declaring scope.
questions.explanation: Divide total array bytes by bytes per element; this does not work on a pointer parameter.

questions.prompt: Which standard type is the result of sizeof?
questions.explanation: sizeof yields size_t, an unsigned integer type.

questions.prompt: Inside void f(int a[10]), what does sizeof a measure?
options: The size of an int pointer
questions.explanation: An array parameter adjusts to a pointer parameter, even when a bound is written.

questions.prompt: Declare a function accepting access to an int array and its size_t element count.
questions.explanation: The pointer supplies access; the separate count supplies the length.

questions.prompt: Which expression measures the entire declared char buffer?
questions.explanation: sizeof an actual array gives its capacity in bytes, independent of string contents.

questions.prompt: What does sizeof(char) always equal in C?
questions.explanation: C measures sizeof in bytes, and a char occupies one byte. A byte need not universally have eight bits.

questions.prompt: Which statement about sizeof *p is correct for int *p?
options: It uses the int type without reading *p
It always dereferences p at runtime
It requires malloc to have run first
questions.explanation: For this non-VLA type, sizeof does not evaluate its operand.

questions.prompt: Which parameter declaration is adjusted to char *s in a function definition?
questions.explanation: An array parameter declaration adjusts to a pointer to its element type.

questions.prompt: Create a writable array initialized with the string cat.
questions.explanation: An array initialized from the literal receives its own writable characters and terminator.

questions.prompt: Write a null terminator at buffer index n, which is within capacity.
questions.explanation: Assign the null character to the element where the string should end.

questions.prompt: Which condition tests for the end of a valid string at index i?
questions.explanation: The string ends at its first character with value zero.

questions.prompt: Which condition continues while s[i] is a non-null character?
questions.explanation: EOF is an input status value, not the terminator of a C string.

questions.prompt: Declare space for at most 15 visible characters plus a string terminator.
questions.explanation: A string needs one extra char for its null terminator.

questions.prompt: Which creates an empty C string in a writable four-byte buffer?
questions.explanation: The first character is zero, so the string’s length is zero.

questions.prompt: Replace the second character of a writable string s with X.
questions.explanation: Use a character constant and zero-based indexing.

questions.prompt: Given char *p pointing into a valid string, move to its next character.
questions.explanation: Increment the pointer to advance; ++*p changes the character value.

questions.prompt: Given a decimal digit character ch, get its numeric digit value.
questions.explanation: The decimal digit characters are consecutive in C’s execution character set.

questions.prompt: Given int digit in 0..9, form the corresponding character.
questions.explanation: Adding the digit value to the character code for zero forms the desired digit character.

questions.prompt: Print an int x in decimal.
questions.explanation: %d expects an int value, not its address.

questions.prompt: Print unsigned int flags in decimal.
questions.explanation: %u matches unsigned int.

questions.prompt: Print unsigned int flags in lowercase hexadecimal.
questions.explanation: %x uses lowercase hexadecimal digits; %X uses uppercase digits.

questions.prompt: Print a size_t count in decimal.
questions.explanation: z is the size_t length modifier; u requests unsigned decimal output.

questions.prompt: Print a valid null-terminated string s.
questions.explanation: %s expects a pointer to the first character; a fixed format avoids treating input as a format string.

questions.prompt: Print a single char ch.
questions.explanation: The char is promoted to int when passed to printf; %c prints a character.

questions.prompt: Print a double value x using fixed-point notation.
questions.explanation: printf %f expects double. A float argument would also promote to double.

questions.prompt: Print an object pointer p with the %p conversion.
questions.explanation: %p requires a void * argument; use an explicit conversion for the variadic call.

questions.prompt: Print one literal percent sign using printf.
questions.explanation: %% in a printf format emits a literal percent sign and consumes no argument.

questions.prompt: Print x followed by a newline.
questions.explanation: Use the newline escape inside the format string.

questions.prompt: Print a long long value x as signed decimal.
questions.explanation: ll selects long long and d requests signed decimal.

questions.prompt: Print integers x then y in that order, separated by a space.
questions.explanation: Conversions consume arguments in the order they appear in the argument list.

questions.prompt: Read decimal input into int x.
questions.explanation: %d requires an int * destination.

questions.prompt: Read hexadecimal input into unsigned int temp.
questions.explanation: %x requires unsigned int *; scanf accepts hexadecimal text with or without 0x.

questions.prompt: Read unsigned decimal input into unsigned int count.
questions.explanation: Use %u for an unsigned int destination.

questions.prompt: Read decimal input into size_t count.
questions.explanation: %zu matches size_t * as the destination.

questions.prompt: Read a floating value into float x.
questions.explanation: scanf %f needs float *; this differs from printf’s promoted double argument.

questions.prompt: Read a floating value into double x.
questions.explanation: scanf %lf needs double *.

questions.prompt: Read one char into ch while first skipping whitespace.
questions.explanation: Leading whitespace in the format consumes input whitespace; %c alone does not skip it.

questions.prompt: Read a whitespace-delimited word safely into char word[16].
questions.explanation: A width of 15 leaves space for the null terminator. The array converts to char *.

questions.prompt: Verify that scanf assigned one requested int.
questions.explanation: Test the number of successful assignments. EOF is also nonzero, so != 0 is insufficient.

questions.prompt: Verify that two requested int conversions both succeeded.
questions.explanation: The return value counts successful assignments, not characters or format tokens.

questions.prompt: Read hexadecimal input directly into unsigned char byte using the correct length modifier.
questions.explanation: hh changes the destination for x to unsigned char *. Input must be representable in that type.

questions.prompt: Read an integer but discard it without supplying a destination pointer.
questions.explanation: An asterisk after % suppresses assignment for that conversion; it does not contribute to the assignment count.

questions.prompt: Read a line into the actual char array buffer[80], respecting its capacity.
questions.explanation: fgets takes destination, capacity, stream; it reads at most capacity minus one characters.

questions.prompt: Which check detects that fgets returned a string successfully?
questions.explanation: fgets returns the buffer pointer on success, NULL on EOF before any characters or on error.

questions.prompt: Which type should hold getchar’s result so it can represent every unsigned-char value and EOF?
questions.explanation: Keep the result in int until after comparing it with EOF.

questions.prompt: Write one character ch to standard output.
questions.explanation: putchar receives the character value as an int.

questions.prompt: Write an error message to the standard error stream.
questions.explanation: fprintf takes a stream before its format string.

questions.prompt: Parse an int from the null-terminated string text into x.
questions.explanation: sscanf reads from a string; its remaining format and pointer arguments follow scanf rules.

questions.prompt: Print a string s followed by a newline with one library call.
questions.explanation: puts writes a string and appends a newline; it does not treat s as a format string.

questions.prompt: Which escape can be used with strcspn to locate a newline in a string buffer?
questions.explanation: strcspn expects a string of rejected characters, so use a double-quoted string containing the newline.

questions.prompt: Allocate exactly sizeof(int) bytes using the pointed-to type of int *p.
questions.explanation: sizeof *p measures the target int without reading it.

questions.prompt: Allocate exactly n times the size of the int pointed to by p, assuming n > 0 and no size multiplication overflow.
questions.explanation: Multiply the element count by the size of one element.

questions.prompt: Use calloc with element count n first and the size of the int pointed to by p second; n is valid and positive.
questions.explanation: calloc takes element count and element size, and initializes every allocated bit to zero.

questions.prompt: In calloc(count, size), what does the second argument specify?
questions.explanation: The allocation size is count multiplied by bytes per element.

questions.prompt: In calloc(4, 2), what does the first argument specify?
questions.explanation: The arguments describe four elements of two bytes each; the returned storage has no stored C array-length metadata.

questions.prompt: Check malloc failure before accessing p.
questions.explanation: Compare the returned pointer with NULL; do not dereference it to test failure.

questions.prompt: Release the allocation whose original returned address is held in p.
questions.explanation: Pass the allocated pointer value to free, exactly once for that allocation.

questions.prompt: After freeing p, explicitly make this pointer variable null.
questions.explanation: Assigning NULL changes p; free does not automatically change pointer variables or other aliases.

questions.prompt: Choose the resize pattern that preserves p if realloc fails; bytes is positive.
options:
int *tmp = realloc(p, bytes);
if (tmp != NULL) p = tmp;
questions.explanation: On failure realloc leaves the old allocation intact; retain its pointer until success.

questions.prompt: Which argument order is correct for realloc?
questions.explanation: realloc accepts an existing allocation pointer and the requested new total byte size.

questions.prompt: Which call is defined and does nothing?
options: free(&local); /* local is an automatic int */
questions.explanation: free(NULL) is explicitly permitted. Stack addresses and already-freed pointers are not valid arguments.

questions.prompt: Which condition guards n * sizeof *p from overflowing size_t before allocation?
questions.explanation: Check with division before performing the multiplication; SIZE_MAX is available from stdint.h.

questions.prompt: Set the first n bytes of valid buffer to zero.
questions.explanation: The arguments are destination, byte value, byte count.

questions.prompt: Fill every byte of an actual unsigned char array data with zero.
questions.explanation: sizeof data measures the whole array here; sizeof *data measures one element.

questions.prompt: Copy n bytes from src to dst, where the regions do not overlap.
questions.explanation: memcpy takes destination first, source second and byte count third.

questions.prompt: Move n bytes from src to dst when the regions may overlap.
questions.explanation: memmove handles overlap. memcpy’s contract requires non-overlapping regions.

questions.prompt: Test whether two valid byte regions compare equal over n bytes.
questions.explanation: memcmp returns zero for equal compared bytes.

questions.prompt: Access generic writable storage one byte at a time through void *mem.
questions.explanation: C permits conversion from void * to an object pointer; character pointers provide byte access.

questions.prompt: Return the original destination pointer from a memset-like function declared void *fill(void *dst, int byte, size_t n).
questions.explanation: The return contract is a pointer, and a memset-like function returns its original destination.

questions.prompt: Convert a fill value to the unsigned-char value used for byte writes.
questions.explanation: A cast to unsigned char obtains the byte value; adding * would cast to a pointer type.

questions.prompt: Get the number of characters before the null terminator in valid string s.
questions.explanation: strlen returns size_t and counts characters before the first null character.

questions.prompt: Test whether strings a and b have equal contents.
questions.explanation: strcmp compares string contents; pointer equality and first-character equality are different tests.

questions.prompt: Copy valid string src including its terminator into sufficiently large, non-overlapping dst.
questions.explanation: strcpy takes destination then source and requires enough capacity for the terminator.

questions.prompt: Append src to an existing string dst with sufficient space and no overlap.
questions.explanation: strcat appends at the end of dst; strcpy replaces its existing contents.

questions.prompt: Locate the first occurrence of character ch in a valid string s.
questions.explanation: strchr searches for one character and returns a pointer or NULL.

questions.prompt: Locate the first occurrence of string needle inside string haystack.
questions.explanation: strstr searches for a substring; its first argument is the string being searched.

questions.prompt: Compare at most n initial characters of strings a and b.
questions.explanation: strncmp takes a maximum comparison count and also stops at a null character.

questions.prompt: For char dst[16], what must be done after strncpy(dst, src, sizeof dst - 1) to guarantee termination?
questions.explanation: strncpy may leave no null terminator when the source reaches the copy limit; explicitly terminate within bounds.

questions.prompt: Strip a newline from a successfully read string buffer using strcspn.
questions.explanation: strcspn yields the first newline index, or the existing terminator index if no newline occurs.

questions.prompt: Which header declares strlen, strcmp and strcpy?
questions.explanation: The standard string and byte-memory functions are declared in string.h.

questions.prompt: Define a struct type with one int member named value.
questions.explanation: A struct definition uses braces around member declarations and a trailing semicolon.

questions.prompt: Declare an object item using an existing tag struct Item.
questions.explanation: A structure tag uses the struct keyword unless a typedef alias has been declared.

questions.prompt: Access member value through struct Item object item.
questions.explanation: Use the dot operator when the left operand is the structure object.

questions.prompt: Access member value through struct Item *p.
questions.explanation: The arrow operator follows the pointer and accesses the member.

questions.prompt: Which expression is equivalent to p->value?
questions.explanation: Parentheses are needed because . binds more tightly than unary *.

questions.prompt: Assign 7 to the value member through struct Item *p.
questions.explanation: p->value names the member object, so assign directly to it.

questions.prompt: Take the address of item’s int value member.
questions.explanation: Apply address-of to the member expression.

questions.prompt: Initialize value to 7 using a designated struct initializer.
questions.explanation: Designated member initializers use .member = expression inside braces.

questions.prompt: Copy all members of struct Item object b into object a.
questions.explanation: Assignment between compatible structure objects is valid; pointer members copy their pointer values.

questions.prompt: Allocate exactly the byte size of one struct Item through the pointed-to type of struct Item *p.
questions.explanation: Use the size of the pointed-to structure, not the pointer object.

questions.prompt: Create byte as an alias for unsigned char.
questions.explanation: A typedef uses a declaration with the alias in the declarator position.

questions.prompt: Create Item as an alias for struct Item.
questions.explanation: The final Item is the typedef name; the earlier Item is the struct tag.

questions.prompt: Define an enum tag Color with constants RED and BLUE.
questions.explanation: Enumerators are comma-separated inside braces.

questions.prompt: Assign the explicit integer value 3 to an enumerator.
questions.explanation: Enumerator initializers use = followed by an integer constant expression.

questions.prompt: Declare variable state using an enum tag State.
questions.explanation: Use enum plus the tag, unless an alias was separately introduced.

questions.prompt: Given typedef int *IntPtr, declare p and q as pointers to int using that alias.
questions.explanation: Both declarators use the pointer typedef; adding another star would add a pointer layer.

questions.prompt: Which header provides bool, true and false for C17 code?
questions.explanation: stdbool.h provides these C17 macros; _Bool is the underlying language type.

questions.prompt: Declare a Boolean flag initialized to true after including stdbool.h.
questions.explanation: C is case-sensitive; bool and true are lowercase C17 header macros.

questions.prompt: Declare next inside struct Node so it can point to another Node.
questions.explanation: A pointer may refer to an incomplete struct type; directly containing the same structure would require infinite size.

questions.prompt: Move struct Node *p to the node named by its next member.
questions.explanation: Follow the stored link. Nodes need not be adjacent in an array.

questions.prompt: Stop traversal when node pointer p is null.
questions.explanation: Test the pointer before accessing its members.

questions.prompt: Initialize a new node’s next link to the current head.
questions.explanation: The next field and head both have pointer-to-node type.

questions.prompt: After node->next = head, make node the list head.
questions.explanation: Update the head pointer to the new node.

questions.prompt: Update the caller’s head through struct Node **headp.
questions.explanation: The caller’s pointer object is reached with one dereference of headp.

questions.prompt: Test whether two node pointers p and target identify the same node.
questions.explanation: Identity compares addresses. Equal member values do not imply the same node.

questions.prompt: Save a node’s successor before freeing that node.
questions.explanation: Read the link before ending the current node’s lifetime.

questions.prompt: Apply bit-by-bit AND to unsigned x and mask.
questions.explanation: A single & performs bitwise AND; && computes logical truth.

questions.prompt: Apply bit-by-bit OR to unsigned x and mask.
questions.explanation: A single | performs bitwise OR.

questions.prompt: Apply bit-by-bit exclusive OR.
questions.explanation: ^ toggles bits where the mask contains ones.

questions.prompt: Complement every bit of unsigned int x.
questions.explanation: ~ is bitwise NOT; ! is logical NOT.

questions.prompt: Shift unsigned x left by k positions.
questions.explanation: << is left shift. The count must be within the promoted type width.

questions.prompt: Shift unsigned x right by k positions.
questions.explanation: >> is right shift; for unsigned values, vacated high bits are zero.

questions.prompt: Shift unsigned x left by k and store the result in x.
questions.explanation: <<= combines shift and assignment.

questions.prompt: Shift unsigned x right by k and store the result in x.
questions.explanation: >>= combines right shift and assignment.

questions.prompt: Select an unsigned left operand when building a mask at bit k.
questions.explanation: The u suffix makes the small literal unsigned int; a plain 1 is int.

questions.prompt: For 32-bit unsigned int, which condition makes a signed int shift count k valid?
questions.explanation: A shift count must be nonnegative and strictly below the promoted left operand width.

questions.prompt: Build a mask with exactly bit k set; bit 0 is the LSB and 0 <= k < 32.
questions.explanation: Shift a single unsigned one to position k.

questions.prompt: Set bit k of unsigned int x, preserving all other bits. Bit 0 is the LSB; 0 <= k < 32.
questions.explanation: OR with a one-bit mask forces only that bit to one.

questions.prompt: Clear bit k of unsigned int x, preserving all other bits. Bit 0 is the LSB; 0 <= k < 32.
questions.explanation: The complemented mask has a zero at k and ones elsewhere; AND clears only k.

questions.prompt: Toggle bit k of unsigned int x. Bit 0 is the LSB; 0 <= k < 32.
questions.explanation: XOR flips the target bit and preserves bits under zero mask positions.

questions.prompt: Read bit k of unsigned int x as exactly 0 or 1. Bit 0 is the LSB; 0 <= k < 32.
questions.explanation: Shift the chosen bit to bit zero, then mask away the others.

questions.prompt: Test whether bit k of unsigned int x is set. Bit 0 is the LSB; 0 <= k < 32.
questions.explanation: Compare the masked result with zero; a set bit above bit zero has a value other than one.

questions.prompt: Set every bit selected by unsigned mask m in x.
questions.explanation: OR sets all mask-selected bits.

questions.prompt: Clear every bit selected by unsigned mask m in x.
questions.explanation: AND with the complemented mask preserves unselected bits.

questions.prompt: Toggle every bit selected by unsigned mask m in x.
questions.explanation: XOR flips selected bits regardless of their prior state.

questions.prompt: Test whether every bit selected by m is set in x.
questions.explanation: All selected bits must survive the AND; unselected bits in x may have either value.

questions.prompt: Keep only the low eight bits of unsigned int x.
questions.explanation: 0xFF has ones only in its low eight bit positions.

questions.prompt: Build a low-k-bit mask for unsigned int, where 0 <= k <= 31.
questions.explanation: Subtracting one fills the k low bits. k = 0 yields zero and does not shift by a negative count.

questions.prompt: Extract bits 7 through 4 of unsigned x into result bits 3 through 0; bit 0 is the LSB.
questions.explanation: Move the upper nibble down four places, then keep four bits.

questions.prompt: Extract w bits starting at LSB-based bit k of unsigned x. Assume 1 <= w <= 31 and k + w <= 32.
questions.explanation: The shift chooses the field’s starting position; the mask chooses its width.

questions.prompt: Append bit b (0 or 1) at the low end of unsigned accumulator value.
questions.explanation: Make room by shifting left, then insert the next bit with OR.

questions.prompt: Select the byte containing nonnegative global bit position p in an eight-bit-byte array.
questions.explanation: Integer division gives the byte index.

questions.prompt: Obtain the offset within an eight-bit byte for nonnegative global position p.
questions.explanation: The remainder gives an offset from zero through seven.

questions.prompt: An unsigned char array data uses eight-bit bytes, with global bit 0 at data[0]’s LSB and LSB-first order in each byte. Read valid global position p as 0 or 1.
questions.explanation: LSB-first numbering uses the within-byte offset directly as the right-shift count.

questions.prompt: An unsigned char array data uses eight-bit bytes, with global bit 0 at data[0]’s MSB and MSB-first order in each byte. Read valid global position p as 0 or 1.
questions.explanation: MSB-first offset zero requires a shift of seven.

questions.prompt: Given size_t pos, width and total with pos <= total, check whether width bytes fit after pos without risking arithmetic overflow.
questions.explanation: The subtraction is safe under the stated bound and avoids overflowing pos + width.

questions.prompt: Clear and replace an unsigned field selected by mask, where bits is already shifted and contains no ones outside mask.
questions.explanation: Clear the old field first, then insert the replacement bits.

questions.prompt: Test the sign bit of an L-bit two’s-complement pattern stored in unsigned raw. Bit 0 is the LSB; 1 <= L <= 31.
questions.explanation: The sign bit is the highest of the L stored bits, at position L - 1.

questions.prompt: Convert int x to double with an explicit cast.
questions.explanation: C casts place a parenthesized type before an expression.

questions.prompt: Divide two ints a and nonzero b using floating-point division.
questions.explanation: Convert an operand before division; casting the completed integer quotient is too late.

questions.prompt: Convert a successfully read unsigned int temp to an unsigned byte.
questions.explanation: A cast to the scalar type converts its value; a star denotes a pointer cast.

questions.prompt: In C17, an eight-bit unsigned char on a machine with 32-bit int is first promoted to which type for arithmetic?
questions.explanation: All 0..255 values fit in int in this model, so integer promotion chooses int.

questions.prompt: Which cast forces an operand x into unsigned int arithmetic?
questions.explanation: The scalar cast changes x’s arithmetic type; pointer casts do not perform the same operation.

questions.prompt: A negative L-bit pattern is in the low L bits of unsigned raw, with 1 <= L <= 31. Select the expression guaranteed to produce the signed int value in C17 with 32-bit int, without an out-of-range unsigned-to-signed conversion.
questions.explanation: Compute raw minus 2^L in a wide signed type, then convert the representable result to int.

questions.prompt: Select the literal whose suffix explicitly makes a small value unsigned long long.
questions.explanation: U and LL combine to request unsigned long long; ULL and LLU are valid suffix orderings.

questions.prompt: Which statement is guaranteed about plain char in C17?
options: Its signedness depends on the implementation
It is the same type as int
questions.explanation: Use signed char or unsigned char explicitly when that distinction matters.

questions.prompt: Include the standard declarations for printf and scanf.
questions.explanation: A standard header name is enclosed in angle brackets after #include.

questions.prompt: Include a project header named helpers.h using the quoted form.
questions.explanation: Quoted header syntax is commonly used for project headers.

questions.prompt: Include standard declarations for malloc, calloc, realloc and free.
questions.explanation: These allocation functions are declared in stdlib.h.

questions.prompt: Include standard declarations for memset, memcpy and memmove.
questions.explanation: The standard byte-memory functions are declared in string.h.

questions.prompt: Define an object-like macro LIMIT with replacement text 16.
questions.explanation: A macro definition has no assignment sign or automatic statement semicolon.

questions.prompt: Start a guard that checks whether HELPERS_H has not been defined.
questions.explanation: #ifndef tests absence of a macro definition.

questions.prompt: Define the guard macro inside #ifndef HELPERS_H.
questions.explanation: Define the same macro so later inclusions skip the guarded content.

questions.prompt: Close a preprocessing conditional such as #ifndef.
questions.explanation: #endif closes the conditional preprocessing group.

questions.prompt: Which header provides size_t and NULL without also requiring an I/O API?
questions.explanation: stddef.h supplies common definitions such as size_t, ptrdiff_t and NULL.

questions.prompt: Which header provides INT_MAX and CHAR_BIT?
questions.explanation: limits.h describes integer implementation limits and bits per byte.

questions.prompt: Which header provides uint32_t when the implementation has that exact-width type?
questions.explanation: stdint.h declares fixed-width integer types when the implementation supports them.

questions.prompt: Remove a macro definition for LIMIT.
questions.explanation: #undef removes the macro definition rather than changing its replacement text.

questions.prompt: Declare a global int defined in a different source file, without defining a new object here.
questions.explanation: extern without an initializer declares an object whose definition may appear elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Give a file-scope int variable internal linkage.
questions.explanation: At file scope, static limits linkage to the translation unit.

questions.prompt: Make a local counter retain its value across calls.
questions.explanation: A static local object has static storage duration; its initializer is not rerun on each call.

questions.prompt: Make a function available only within its translation unit by name.
questions.explanation: static at file scope gives the function internal linkage.

questions.prompt: Compile main.c into an object file without linking, using GCC.
questions.explanation: -c stops after producing object code; -E stops after preprocessing and -S after assembly output.

questions.prompt: Compile and link main.c and helpers.c into an executable named app.
questions.explanation: Provide both source files to the compiler driver and choose the output name with -o.

questions.prompt: Link already compiled main.o and helpers.o into app.
questions.explanation: The compiler driver can invoke the linker on object files.

questions.prompt: Request C17 and the common Wall/Wextra warning groups when building main.c.
questions.explanation: -std=c17 selects the language dialect; -Wall and -Wextra enable useful warning groups.

questions.prompt: Where should a function prototype shared by several C source files normally be placed?
options: In a header included by those source files
Only inside a caller’s function body
In an object file edited as text
In a #define replacing the entire program
questions.explanation: A shared header supplies a consistent declaration to every translation unit.

questions.prompt: Which declaration promises a function exists but supplies no body?
questions.explanation: A function declaration ending in a semicolon is not its implementation.
